title: How you come across in a case interview, and how to improve it
description: The half of the interview most candidates never train: voice, composure and business fluency.
hook: Interviewers are asking themselves a quiet question all the way through your case: would I put this person in front of a client? That is not about being polished or extroverted. It is about being clear, calm and easy to follow. This guide covers the small habits that change how you come across, and how to practise them.
body:
In this guide

  • Why this matters as much as the maths
  • Voice: pace, pauses, no fillers
  • Mind: hold more in your head
  • Fluency and calm
  • A worked example
  • What to remember
  • Check yourself

Why this matters as much as the maths

Two candidates with the same structure can get different results. One speaks in calm, well-paced sentences and pauses before answering. The other rushes, fills silences with "um" and "like", and loses the thread under pressure. The interviewer is picturing you in front of their client. These habits are trainable, in about 10-20 minutes a day.

Voice: pace, pauses, no fillers

  • Paced reading: read a business article aloud slightly slower than feels natural, pausing at every full stop. Five minutes a day.
  • Pause practice: record a 2-minute answer, count your filler words, re-record with a silent pause in place of each one. A pause sounds confident; "um" sounds nervous.
  • Explain to the CEO: explain one concept in 60 seconds, top-down and jargon-free.

Mind: hold more in your head

Mid-case you are juggling the goal, your structure, three numbers and the next step, while talking. Practise the skills you actually use: recap a 2-minute podcast clip in 60 seconds, or redraw a framework from memory. Writing the goal and key numbers at the top of your page also helps you avoid going blank. (Brain-training apps improve the game itself, but there is little evidence they help in interviews.)

Fluency and calm

Read 15 minutes of business press or a strategy book daily, and note one real company story you could use in a case. Before every mock and the real interview, do two minutes of box breathing (in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4). A calm voice starts with calm breathing.

See it in action: The same answer, two ways

Rushed: "So, um, I think like the main thing is basically costs, because, um, the delivery thing, like, they pay a lot of commission and stuff."

Composed: "The main driver is cost. [pause] Specifically, delivery commissions, which grew from 1.5% to 7.6% of revenue."

Same idea. The second one sounds like someone you could put in front of a client.

What to remember

  • Interviewers judge every sentence, not just your structure.
  • Replace filler words with pauses.
  • 10-20 minutes a day of voice and mind practice compounds quickly.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer. Getting some wrong is how it sticks.

1. What is the best replacement for a filler word like "um"?

  • Speaking faster
  • A short silent pause
  • Saying "basically"
Show the answer

A short silent pause. Pauses read as confidence and give you thinking time.

Try it now

Record yourself answering "Why consulting?" for 60 seconds. Play it back and count your filler words (um, like, sort of). Then record it again with a silent pause wherever a filler was.

Give yourself 60 seconds, out loud if you can. Speaking it, rather than thinking it, is what builds the skill.

Show a strong answer

Aim for fewer than 3 fillers a minute. A clean shape: one-sentence answer, two reasons each backed by a moment from your own experience, and a close that links to the firm you’re speaking to.
outro: You do not have to get all of this right at once. Pick one thing from this guide to focus on in your next practice case. This guide is lesson 10 of the free PrepForCase course, where you can do the exercise and quiz and track your progress.
